tip: entendre is hearing that just reaches you; écouter is actively listening. Elle entend un bruit = she hears a noise, unbidden.
'On' is an informal way to say 'we' in spoken French. It conjugates like il/elle (3rd person singular): on mange, on parle.
raconter is "to tell" a story or events, while dire is to say words. Ils racontent une histoire = they tell a story.
For body parts French uses the article, not "my": je lève la main = I raise my hand (literally "the hand"). Ownership is understood.
présenter means to introduce a person, not "present." Tu présentes ton collègue = you introduce your colleague.

english: They take an umbrella with them.
tip: emporter = take something away with you, from here. Ils emportent un parapluie = they take an umbrella along. Bringing toward here is apporter.
pourboire (a tip) is literally "for drink" – pour boire. Je laisse un pourboire = I leave a tip, once money for a drink.
apporter = bring an object toward here; emporter = take it away. Vous apportez le dessert = you bring the dessert. For people, use amener.
louer means both rent AND rent out – tenant and landlord use the same verb. Je loue un appartement = I rent an apartment.
repasser means to iron, but also "to come or pass by again." Il repasse sa chemise = he irons his shirt. Same verb, two lives.
marcher is "to walk," but also "to work/run" for machines: ça marche = it works. Il marche jusqu'à l'école = he walks to school.
Luggage is uncountable in English but plural in French: les bagages always takes a plural article and verb. One bag alone is un bagage.
un costume is a suit, not a costume (that's un déguisement). Tu portes un costume = you wear a suit.
emprunter = to borrow, but with a road it means to take it: nous empruntons ce chemin = we take this path.
embrasser today means to kiss, not "embrace." Tu embrasses ta grand-mère = you kiss your grandmother, on the cheeks.
gagner means both to win and to earn: il gagne le match = he wins the game, but gagner sa vie = earn a living. Context decides.
Son doesn't show the owner's gender – it agrees with the noun. Anniversaire is masculine, so son anniversaire is his OR her birthday alike.
A number stands in for the article: 'deux enfants', never deux des enfants. The count already does the article's job.
Vous is both plural 'you' and the polite singular. 'Vous pouvez répéter ?' is the safe form with a stranger; tu would sound too familiar.
'Je veux un café' is blunt – fine among friends, pushy to a waiter. To order, soften it to 'je voudrais' (I'd like).
You "take" transport with prendre: je prends le train = I take the train. The same verb serves food and drink: prendre un café.
Connaître is knowing-by-familiarity – people, places, songs: 'connais cette chanson'. Knowing a fact or how-to would be savoir.
connaître is knowing by familiarity – people, places: elle connaît bien Paris = knows Paris well. For facts you'd switch to savoir.
un roman is a novel, not anything "Roman." Tu lis un roman = you read a novel. A short story is une nouvelle.
French uses the plain present for near-future plans: je pars demain matin = I'm leaving tomorrow morning. No separate "going to" needed.
vivre and habiter both mean "live," but vivre is broader – to be alive, to reside: je vis à Marseille = I live in Marseille.
Most French adjectives follow the noun, but bon comes before: un bon restaurant = a good restaurant. A small set (good, big, old) leads.
For meals prendre means "to have," not take: nous prenons le petit déjeuner = we have breakfast (literally "little lunch").
'Écouter' means 'to listen to' – the 'to' is built in. No preposition needed: j'écoute la musique (I listen to music).
'Téléphoner à' requires the preposition 'à' before the person: il téléphone à sa mère. Unlike 'appeler' which takes a direct object.
